title: Ezekiel 14:12–23
context: The LORD tells Ezekiel that when a land sins and he sends famine, wild animals, sword, or pestilence, even Noah, Daniel, and Job could deliver only themselves by their righteousness, not their sons or daughters. How much more will this be true when his four severe judgments fall on Jerusalem. Yet some survivors will come out to the exiles, and when the exiles see their ways they will be comforted, knowing that God did not act without cause. The passage concerns a land under judgment. The identity of this Daniel is debated, and the text does not settle it. Both traditions read the passage as shared ground about the justice of God’s judgments.

verses.text: The LORD’s word came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD’s word comes to Ezekiel. A new message on judgment and intercession begins.

Arminian readers see God explaining why judgment on Jerusalem cannot be averted by the righteousness of a few, however outstanding.
verses.reformedNotes:
The message is framed as a general principle and then applied to Jerusalem in verse 21.

Reformed readers see God explaining his justice. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the seriousness of national sin.

verses.text: “Son of man, when a land sins against me by committing a trespass, and I stretch out my hand on it, and break the staff of its bread and send famine on it, and cut off from it man and animal—
verses.arminianNotes:
When a land sins against God by trespass, and he breaks its staff of bread and sends famine, cutting off man and animal, a principle follows. The case is general.

Arminian readers see judgment answering a land’s persistent unfaithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes:
The “staff of bread” pictures the food supply on which life depends.

Reformed readers see God’s rule over provision and famine. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s judgment on a land’s sin.

verses.text: though these three men, Noah, Daniel, and Job, were in it, they would deliver only their own souls by their righteousness,” says the Lord GOD.
verses.arminianNotes:
Even if Noah, Daniel, and Job were in it, they would deliver only their own souls by their righteousness. Their righteousness cannot save others.

Arminian readers see judgment on a land under sentence.
verses.reformedNotes:
Noah is called righteous in Genesis 6:9 and Job blameless in Job 1:1. Some identify Daniel with the exile of the book of Daniel; others suggest an ancient figure of renown (compare 28:3). The text does not settle it.

Reformed readers agree. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: “If I cause evil animals to pass through the land, and they ravage it and it is made desolate, so that no man may pass through because of the animals—
verses.arminianNotes:
If God sends wild animals to ravage the land so that no one can pass through, a second case is posed. The scenario repeats with a new judgment.

Arminian readers see the principle tested against each kind of disaster.
verses.reformedNotes:
Wild animals appear among covenant curses (compare Leviticus 26:22) and among the four judgments of verse 21.

Reformed readers see God sovereign over every means of judgment. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the variety of judgments a land under sentence may face.

verses.text: though these three men were in it, as I live,” says the Lord GOD, “they would deliver neither sons nor daughters. They only would be delivered, but the land would be desolate.
verses.arminianNotes:
Even if the three were there, they would deliver neither sons nor daughters; only they would be delivered. Even family cannot be spared by their righteousness.

Arminian readers see personal righteousness unable to cover others.
verses.reformedNotes:
The mention of sons and daughters may recall that Noah’s family was spared and Job’s children were not.

Reformed readers see the limits of human righteousness for others. Both traditions read this as shared ground about a land under judgment, not about prayer as such.

verses.text: “Or if I bring a sword on that land, and say, ‘Sword, go through the land, so that I cut off from it man and animal’—
verses.arminianNotes:
If God brings the sword on the land and cuts off man and animal, a third case is posed. War is now the judgment.

Arminian readers see the principle extended to invasion and conflict, which Jerusalem was about to face.
verses.reformedNotes:
The command “Sword, go through the land” personifies the sword as God’s agent.

Reformed readers see God directing even warfare. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s sovereignty over the instruments of judgment.

verses.text: though these three men were in it, as I live,” says the Lord GOD, “they would deliver neither sons nor daughters, but they only would be delivered themselves.
verses.arminianNotes:
Even with the three present, they would deliver neither sons nor daughters, but only themselves. The principle is repeated.

Arminian readers see personal accountability emphasized, with no transfer of one person’s righteousness to another.
verses.reformedNotes:
The repetition stresses that the outcome does not change with the type of judgment.

Reformed readers see the consistency of God’s justice. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the limits of others’ righteousness when a land is under judgment.

verses.text: “Or if I send a pestilence into that land, and pour out my wrath on it in blood, to cut off from it man and animal—
verses.arminianNotes:
If God sends pestilence and pours out his wrath in blood, cutting off man and animal, a fourth case is posed. Disease completes the list.

Arminian readers see judgment answering long-standing rebellion.
verses.reformedNotes:
The four cases of verses 13–19 match the four judgments named in verse 21.

Reformed readers see God’s sovereign justice. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s judgment on a land’s persistent sin, reported here without graphic elaboration.

verses.text: though Noah, Daniel, and Job, were in it, as I live,” says the Lord GOD, “they would deliver neither son nor daughter; they would deliver only their own souls by their righteousness.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Even if Noah, Daniel, and Job were there, they would deliver neither son nor daughter, only their own souls. The principle closes.

Arminian readers see personal righteousness unable to avert judgment on a sinful land.
verses.reformedNotes:
The names are repeated, framing the four cases.

Reformed readers agree that no human righteousness could stay this judgment. Both traditions read this as shared ground about a land under judgment, not a denial of intercession (compare Joshua 10:14).

verses.text: For the Lord GOD says: “How much more when I send my four severe judgments on Jerusalem—the sword, the famine, the evil animals, and the pestilence—to cut off from it man and animal!
verses.arminianNotes:
The Lord GOD says, how much more when he sends his four severe judgments on Jerusalem: sword, famine, evil animals, and pestilence. The principle is applied.

Arminian readers see Jerusalem facing the full measure of judgment.
verses.reformedNotes:
The “four severe judgments” gather the cases of verses 13–19.

Reformed readers see God’s justice fully expressed. Both traditions read this as shared ground and report the verse soberly.

verses.text: Yet, behold, there will be left a remnant in it that will be carried out, both sons and daughters. Behold, they will come out to you, and you will see their way and their doings. Then you will be comforted concerning the evil that I have brought on Jerusalem, even concerning all that I have brought on it.
verses.arminianNotes:
Yet a remnant, sons and daughters, will be brought out and come to the exiles, who will see their ways and be comforted concerning Jerusalem. A surprising remnant appears.

Arminian readers see mercy alongside judgment.
verses.reformedNotes:
The survivors are spared, it seems, not for their righteousness but to show why judgment came.

Reformed readers see God’s purposes in preserving them. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: They will comfort you, when you see their way and their doings; then you will know that I have not done all that I have done in it without cause,” says the Lord GOD.
verses.arminianNotes:
The survivors will comfort the exiles, who will see their ways and know that God has not acted without cause. Judgment is shown to be just.

Arminian readers see God vindicating his justice before the exiles.
verses.reformedNotes:
The comfort lies in understanding that the judgment was deserved.

Reformed readers see God’s justice displayed. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s judgments being righteous and purposeful, and about the exiles coming to see that God was just.
